questions.stem: This figure shows a repertoire of lymphocytes each bearing a distinct antigen receptor (a, b, c, x, y, z). Antigen X appears and engages only the lymphocyte bearing receptor x, which then proliferates into a clone secreting anti-X antibody. According to the principle this illustrates, when is a lymphocyte's antigen specificity determined?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After antigen exposure, when the antigen instructs the receptor to fold around it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Randomly re-assigned each time the cell divides

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only after the lymphocyte fuses with the antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: By the concentration of antigen present at the time of binding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Before antigen exposure; each lymphocyte's receptor specificity is predetermined

explanation.summary: The figure illustrates clonal selection. A vast repertoire of lymphocytes, each with a unique pre-formed receptor, exists before any antigen is encountered. Antigen does not instruct receptor shape; it simply selects and activates the pre-existing clone whose receptor already fits, driving that clone's proliferation and antibody production. This refutes the older instructional theory of antibody formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure illustrates clonal selection. A vast repertoire of lymphocytes, each with a unique pre-formed receptor, exists before any antigen is encountered. Antigen does not instruct receptor shape; it simply selects and activates the pre-existing clone whose receptor already fits, driving that clone's proliferation and antibody production. This refutes the older instructional theory of antibody formation.

questions.stem: This figure shows antigen-bound B cells being sorted by the strength of antigen binding: those with lower-affinity receptors die, while those with higher-affinity receptors preferentially survive and proliferate, progressively improving the average affinity of the response. Which molecular process generates the receptor variants that are then selected in this way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: V(D)J recombination in the bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isotype (class) switching of the heavy-chain constant region

choices.label: C
choices.text: Somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin variable-region genes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Allelic exclusion of the light-chain locus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gene conversion of MHC class II alleles

explanation.summary: The figure depicts affinity maturation. In the germinal center, activation-induced cytidine deaminase drives somatic hypermutation, introducing point mutations into the immunoglobulin variable regions. B cells whose mutated receptors bind antigen with higher affinity are preferentially selected to survive and proliferate, while lower-affinity clones undergo apoptosis. Class switching changes isotype/effector function but not affinity; V(D)J recombination creates the initial repertoire, not the fine-tuned variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure depicts affinity maturation. In the germinal center, activation-induced cytidine deaminase drives somatic hypermutation, introducing point mutations into the immunoglobulin variable regions. B cells whose mutated receptors bind antigen with higher affinity are preferentially selected to survive and proliferate, while lower-affinity clones undergo apoptosis. Class switching changes isotype/effector function but not affinity; V(D)J recombination creates the initial repertoire, not the fine-tuned variants.

questions.stem: This diagram labels the regions of an immunoglobulin monomer, including the antigen-binding (Fab) arms, the hinge, and the crystallizable (Fc) region. The protease papain cleaves the antibody at the hinge. What fragments result from papain digestion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment

choices.label: B
choices.text: One Fab fragment and two Fc fragments

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two separate heavy chains and two light chains

choices.label: D
choices.text: One F(ab')2 fragment and one Fc fragment

explanation.summary: Papain cleaves the immunoglobulin on the amino-terminal side of the hinge disulfide bonds, yielding two identical monovalent Fab fragments (each with one antigen-binding site) and one Fc fragment (which mediates effector functions and binds complement/Fc receptors). Pepsin, in contrast, cleaves below the hinge to give a single divalent F(ab')2 fragment plus a degraded Fc.
explanation.whyCorrect: Papain cleaves the immunoglobulin on the amino-terminal side of the hinge disulfide bonds, yielding two identical monovalent Fab fragments (each with one antigen-binding site) and one Fc fragment (which mediates effector functions and binds complement/Fc receptors). Pepsin, in contrast, cleaves below the hinge to give a single divalent F(ab')2 fragment plus a degraded Fc.

questions.stem: This table lists mechanisms that expand the antigen-receptor repertoire, distinguishing combinatorial diversity from junctional diversity, and shows that adding or removing nucleotides at the segment joins vastly increases the total potential repertoire. Which enzyme adds the non-templated (N-region) nucleotides at these junctions?

explanation.summary: Junctional diversity arises when segment ends are trimmed and when non-templated nucleotides are inserted at the V(D)J joins. Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) adds these N-region nucleotides, greatly increasing repertoire diversity (raising Ig from ~10^6 to ~10^11 combinations). RAG1/2 cut the DNA to initiate recombination but do not add N-nucleotides; AID drives somatic hypermutation and class switching later in mature B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Junctional diversity arises when segment ends are trimmed and when non-templated nucleotides are inserted at the V(D)J joins. Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) adds these N-region nucleotides, greatly increasing repertoire diversity (raising Ig from ~10^6 to ~10^11 combinations). RAG1/2 cut the DNA to initiate recombination but do not add N-nucleotides; AID drives somatic hypermutation and class switching later in mature B cells.

questions.stem: This figure shows both a schematic (A) and a ribbon structure (B) of a heterodimeric antigen receptor composed of two disulfide-linked chains, each with a membrane-distal variable (V) domain and a membrane-proximal constant (C) domain anchored in the membrane. This receptor is found on the surface of which cell?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mast cell (this is the high-affinity IgE receptor)

choices.label: C
choices.text: T cell (this is the alpha-beta T-cell receptor)

explanation.summary: The two disulfide-linked chains each contain one variable and one constant immunoglobulin-like domain, identifying the alpha-beta T-cell receptor. The variable domains (Valpha/Vbeta) form the antigen-binding site that recognizes peptide presented on MHC. Unlike membrane immunoglobulin on B cells, the TCR is not secreted and recognizes only processed peptide-MHC, not soluble native antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The two disulfide-linked chains each contain one variable and one constant immunoglobulin-like domain, identifying the alpha-beta T-cell receptor. The variable domains (Valpha/Vbeta) form the antigen-binding site that recognizes peptide presented on MHC. Unlike membrane immunoglobulin on B cells, the TCR is not secreted and recognizes only processed peptide-MHC, not soluble native antigen.

questions.stem: This figure shows three effector functions of antibodies: coating bacteria to promote uptake by a macrophage; blocking a microbe from attaching to epithelial cells; and depositing C3b/forming a membrane attack complex. The membrane attack complex generated in the right-hand panel kills the target microbe by which mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking the microbe's adhesion to host cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-linking Fc receptors to trigger degranulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Triggering caspase-mediated apoptosis of the microbe

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forming a transmembrane pore that causes osmotic lysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enhancing antigen presentation on MHC class I

explanation.summary: The panels show opsonization, neutralization, and complement activation. Antibody-triggered classical complement activation deposits C3b (an opsonin) and assembles the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), which inserts into the microbial membrane forming a pore. The resulting loss of osmotic integrity causes lysis. Neutralization (blocking adhesion) and opsonization are the other, distinct functions shown.
explanation.whyCorrect: The panels show opsonization, neutralization, and complement activation. Antibody-triggered classical complement activation deposits C3b (an opsonin) and assembles the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), which inserts into the microbial membrane forming a pore. The resulting loss of osmotic integrity causes lysis. Neutralization (blocking adhesion) and opsonization are the other, distinct functions shown.

questions.stem: This diagram shows an antibody built from five four-chain monomer units held together in a radial arrangement by a central joining (J) chain and disulfide bonds. Which immunoglobulin isotype has this structure?

explanation.summary: A pentamer of five monomers linked by a J chain is the classic structure of secreted IgM, giving it 10 potential antigen-binding sites and making it a highly efficient complement activator. IgM is the first antibody produced in a primary response. Secretory IgA is a dimer with a secretory component; IgG, IgE, and IgD circulate as monomers.
explanation.whyCorrect: A pentamer of five monomers linked by a J chain is the classic structure of secreted IgM, giving it 10 potential antigen-binding sites and making it a highly efficient complement activator. IgM is the first antibody produced in a primary response. Secretory IgA is a dimer with a secretory component; IgG, IgE, and IgD circulate as monomers.

questions.stem: This figure shows germline-to-rearranged DNA for the two chains of the T-cell receptor, one encoded on chromosome 14 and the other on chromosome 7, assembled to form the mature receptor protein. Which gene segment is present in the rearrangement of the beta chain (bottom) but absent from the alpha chain (top)?

explanation.summary: The TCR alpha chain is assembled from V and J segments joined to C, whereas the beta chain uses V, D, and J segments joined to C. The additional diversity (D) segment, combined with junctional diversity at the extra join, increases the combinatorial and junctional diversity of the beta chain. This parallels immunoglobulin heavy versus light chain assembly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The TCR alpha chain is assembled from V and J segments joined to C, whereas the beta chain uses V, D, and J segments joined to C. The additional diversity (D) segment, combined with junctional diversity at the extra join, increases the combinatorial and junctional diversity of the beta chain. This parallels immunoglobulin heavy versus light chain assembly.

questions.stem: This diagram shows two antibody monomers joined tail-to-tail by a joining (J) chain and wrapped by an additional polypeptide (secretory component) acquired during transport across epithelium. This form of antibody predominates in which location?

choices.label: A
choices.text: On naive B cells as the primary surface receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: The intravascular compartment as the main serum antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: On the surface of mast cells and basophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mucosal secretions such as saliva, tears, and breast milk

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within the cytosol of infected cells

explanation.summary: The figure shows secretory IgA: a dimer linked by a J chain and stabilized by the secretory component added as it is transcytosed across mucosal epithelium. Secretory IgA is the dominant antibody at mucosal surfaces and in breast milk, where it neutralizes pathogens and toxins. IgG dominates serum, IgE binds mast cells, and IgM/IgD are the main surface receptors on naive B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure shows secretory IgA: a dimer linked by a J chain and stabilized by the secretory component added as it is transcytosed across mucosal epithelium. Secretory IgA is the dominant antibody at mucosal surfaces and in breast milk, where it neutralizes pathogens and toxins. IgG dominates serum, IgE binds mast cells, and IgM/IgD are the main surface receptors on naive B cells.

questions.stem: This figure shows a follicular helper T cell interacting with an activated B cell that has already bound antigen through its B-cell receptor. In addition to TCR recognition of peptide on the B cell's MHC class II, the B cell receives a critical second signal from the T cell. Which receptor-ligand interaction provides this second signal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PD-L1 on the B cell binding PD-1 on the T cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: ICAM-1 on the B cell binding LFA-1 on the T cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: B7 on the B cell binding CD28 on the T cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD40 on the B cell binding CD40 ligand on the T cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fas on the B cell binding Fas ligand on the T cell

explanation.summary: In T-dependent B-cell activation, the B cell presents antigen on MHC class II to a helper (Tfh) cell; the licensed T cell then delivers CD40L, which engages CD40 on the B cell, and secretes cytokines. CD40-CD40L signaling is essential for B-cell proliferation, germinal center formation, isotype switching, and affinity maturation. Loss of CD40L causes hyper-IgM syndrome. Fas-FasL signaling promotes apoptosis, the opposite outcome.
explanation.whyCorrect: In T-dependent B-cell activation, the B cell presents antigen on MHC class II to a helper (Tfh) cell; the licensed T cell then delivers CD40L, which engages CD40 on the B cell, and secretes cytokines. CD40-CD40L signaling is essential for B-cell proliferation, germinal center formation, isotype switching, and affinity maturation. Loss of CD40L causes hyper-IgM syndrome. Fas-FasL signaling promotes apoptosis, the opposite outcome.

questions.stem: This figure shows a naive B cell responding to a repetitive polysaccharide antigen (with help from other signals such as complement) and differentiating into short-lived plasma cells that secrete mainly low-affinity IgM, without a germinal center. What type of humoral response does this represent?

explanation.summary: Repetitive polysaccharide antigens can crosslink many B-cell receptors and, with second signals like complement C3d, activate B cells without T-cell help. This T-independent response yields predominantly low-affinity IgM from short-lived plasma cells, with little class switching, affinity maturation, or memory. Because young children mount T-independent responses poorly, encapsulated-organism polysaccharide vaccines are conjugated to protein to recruit T-cell help.
explanation.whyCorrect: Repetitive polysaccharide antigens can crosslink many B-cell receptors and, with second signals like complement C3d, activate B cells without T-cell help. This T-independent response yields predominantly low-affinity IgM from short-lived plasma cells, with little class switching, affinity maturation, or memory. Because young children mount T-independent responses poorly, encapsulated-organism polysaccharide vaccines are conjugated to protein to recruit T-cell help.

questions.stem: This graph plots two antibody classes over time after a primary immunization and a later secondary immunization with the same antigen. Compared with the primary response, the secondary response is faster, larger, and dominated by the isotype that peaks highest after re-exposure. Which cells are chiefly responsible for this more rapid and robust secondary response?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Naive B cells newly emerging from the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Memory B cells generated during the primary response

explanation.summary: The graph shows IgM dominating the slower primary response, while the secondary response rises faster and higher and is dominated by IgG. This anamnestic response is mediated by long-lived memory B cells (and memory T cells) generated during the primary exposure; upon re-encounter they rapidly proliferate and differentiate into class-switched, high-affinity IgG-secreting plasma cells. This principle underlies vaccine booster dosing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The graph shows IgM dominating the slower primary response, while the secondary response rises faster and higher and is dominated by IgG. This anamnestic response is mediated by long-lived memory B cells (and memory T cells) generated during the primary exposure; upon re-encounter they rapidly proliferate and differentiate into class-switched, high-affinity IgG-secreting plasma cells. This principle underlies vaccine booster dosing.

questions.stem: This figure shows immature B cells, which express complete antigen receptors, undergoing one of two fates in the bone marrow depending on how strongly their receptor binds self-antigen. An immature B cell whose receptor strongly recognizes a self-antigen follows the left-hand pathway. What is its principal fate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Class switching to IgG and export to lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Proliferation into a high-affinity memory clone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immediate differentiation into an antibody-secreting plasma cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conversion into a follicular dendritic cell

explanation.summary: The figure depicts B-cell central tolerance. Immature B cells whose receptors bind self-antigen strongly undergo negative selection, primarily clonal deletion by apoptosis (some instead undergo receptor editing to change specificity). B cells that bind self weakly or not at all are positively selected and mature into the periphery. This screening prevents autoreactive B cells from entering the repertoire.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure depicts B-cell central tolerance. Immature B cells whose receptors bind self-antigen strongly undergo negative selection, primarily clonal deletion by apoptosis (some instead undergo receptor editing to change specificity). B cells that bind self weakly or not at all are positively selected and mature into the periphery. This screening prevents autoreactive B cells from entering the repertoire.

questions.stem: This figure shows the structure and histology of the lymph node and spleen, mapping where different lymphocytes localize. A patient with a hereditary defect in T-cell development (e.g., DiGeorge/thymic aplasia) would show marked depletion of lymphocytes in which lymph node region?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The germinal centers of secondary follicles

choices.label: C
choices.text: The primary follicles of the cortex

explanation.summary: The lymph node paracortex is the T-cell zone (analogous to the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath in the spleen), while follicles/germinal centers in the cortex are B-cell zones and medullary cords contain plasma cells and macrophages. A defect in T-cell production, as in DiGeorge syndrome, selectively depletes the paracortex, whereas B-cell follicles remain relatively preserved. Knowing zone-specific residence lets you predict which region is affected by a given cellular deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lymph node paracortex is the T-cell zone (analogous to the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath in the spleen), while follicles/germinal centers in the cortex are B-cell zones and medullary cords contain plasma cells and macrophages. A defect in T-cell production, as in DiGeorge syndrome, selectively depletes the paracortex, whereas B-cell follicles remain relatively preserved. Knowing zone-specific residence lets you predict which region is affected by a given cellular deficiency.

questions.stem: This figure depicts the reaction occurring in the germinal center, showing B cells proliferating in a dark zone, being selected for improved affinity in a light zone by follicular dendritic cells and Tfh cells, and finally exiting as plasma cells and memory B cells. Which two processes occurring here improve antibody affinity and change antibody isotype, respectively?

explanation.summary: The germinal center is where affinity maturation and isotype switching occur. Somatic hypermutation introduces mutations into variable regions; high-affinity clones are selected by competing for antigen on follicular dendritic cells and for Tfh help. Class-switch recombination changes the heavy-chain constant region (e.g., IgM to IgG/IgA/IgE) without altering specificity. Both depend on activation-induced cytidine deaminase and yield plasma cells and memory B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The germinal center is where affinity maturation and isotype switching occur. Somatic hypermutation introduces mutations into variable regions; high-affinity clones are selected by competing for antigen on follicular dendritic cells and for Tfh help. Class-switch recombination changes the heavy-chain constant region (e.g., IgM to IgG/IgA/IgE) without altering specificity. Both depend on activation-induced cytidine deaminase and yield plasma cells and memory B cells.

questions.stem: This figure follows B-cell development from a hematopoietic stem cell through pro-B, pre-B, and immature B stages in the bone marrow, then into the circulation as a mature naive B cell. The mature naive B cell shown co-expresses surface IgM together with which other immunoglobulin isotype?

explanation.summary: During antigen-independent development in the bone marrow, the pre-B cell expresses a heavy chain and the immature B cell expresses a complete surface IgM (BCR). As it matures and enters the periphery, the naive B cell co-expresses surface IgM and IgD (produced by alternative splicing of the same heavy-chain transcript). Switching to IgG, IgA, or IgE occurs only later, after antigen encounter and class-switch recombination.
explanation.whyCorrect: During antigen-independent development in the bone marrow, the pre-B cell expresses a heavy chain and the immature B cell expresses a complete surface IgM (BCR). As it matures and enters the periphery, the naive B cell co-expresses surface IgM and IgD (produced by alternative splicing of the same heavy-chain transcript). Switching to IgG, IgA, or IgE occurs only later, after antigen encounter and class-switch recombination.

questions.stem: This figure traces the continuous recirculation of lymphocytes among blood, the thoracic duct, secondary lymphoid organs (lymph node and spleen), and mucosal tissues. Through which specialized vascular structure do naive lymphocytes leave the blood to enter a lymph node?

choices.label: E
choices.text: The central arteriole of the white pulp

explanation.summary: Naive lymphocytes exit the blood into lymph nodes by crossing high endothelial venules, using L-selectin, chemokine, and integrin interactions to home into the node. If they do not encounter antigen, they leave via the efferent lymphatic, which drains toward the thoracic duct and back into the blood, sustaining continuous surveillance. Afferent lymphatics carry antigen and dendritic cells into the node, not blood-borne lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Naive lymphocytes exit the blood into lymph nodes by crossing high endothelial venules, using L-selectin, chemokine, and integrin interactions to home into the node. If they do not encounter antigen, they leave via the efferent lymphatic, which drains toward the thoracic duct and back into the blood, sustaining continuous surveillance. Afferent lymphatics carry antigen and dendritic cells into the node, not blood-borne lymphocytes.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation
questions.stem: This figure follows T-cell development from lymphoid progenitors entering the thymus, progressing through double-negative and double-positive stages with V(D)J recombination of the TCR, and emerging as mature single-positive CD4+ or CD8+ T cells that enter the circulation. In which organ does this antigen-independent development and selection of T cells occur?

explanation.summary: Although T-cell progenitors arise in the bone marrow, they migrate to the thymus, where they undergo TCR gene rearrangement and progress from double-negative to double-positive (CD4+CD8+) thymocytes and then to single-positive CD4+ or CD8+ cells. Positive selection occurs in the thymic cortex and negative selection in the medulla. Failure of thymic development (e.g., DiGeorge syndrome) results in absent mature T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although T-cell progenitors arise in the bone marrow, they migrate to the thymus, where they undergo TCR gene rearrangement and progress from double-negative to double-positive (CD4+CD8+) thymocytes and then to single-positive CD4+ or CD8+ cells. Positive selection occurs in the thymic cortex and negative selection in the medulla. Failure of thymic development (e.g., DiGeorge syndrome) results in absent mature T cells.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation
questions.stem: This figure shows double-positive thymocytes in the cortex being tested against self MHC plus peptide. Some weakly recognize MHC and are positively selected, while others fail to recognize any self MHC. What is the fate of a thymocyte whose T-cell receptor cannot recognize self-MHC at all?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Export as a naive CD8+ T cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Differentiation into a natural killer cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negative selection because of strong self-reactivity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maturation into a regulatory T cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Apoptosis due to failed positive selection

explanation.summary: During thymic selection, a double-positive thymocyte must recognize self-MHC weakly to be positively selected (in the cortex). A thymocyte whose TCR cannot engage self-MHC receives no survival signal and dies by neglect. Separately, thymocytes that recognize self-MHC/peptide too strongly are removed by negative selection (apoptosis) in the medulla to enforce central tolerance. Only intermediate-affinity cells survive to become mature CD4+ or CD8+ T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: During thymic selection, a double-positive thymocyte must recognize self-MHC weakly to be positively selected (in the cortex). A thymocyte whose TCR cannot engage self-MHC receives no survival signal and dies by neglect. Separately, thymocytes that recognize self-MHC/peptide too strongly are removed by negative selection (apoptosis) in the medulla to enforce central tolerance. Only intermediate-affinity cells survive to become mature CD4+ or CD8+ T cells.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation
questions.stem: This figure shows a dendritic cell activating a naive T cell, providing both TCR-MHC engagement and a costimulatory interaction. If the naive T cell receives the TCR-MHC signal (signal 1) but the costimulatory signal (signal 2) is absent, what is the usual consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The T cell lyses the dendritic cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: The T cell secretes maximal IL-2 and expands

choices.label: C
choices.text: The T cell is fully activated and proliferates normally

choices.label: D
choices.text: The T cell becomes anergic (functionally unresponsive)

choices.label: E
choices.text: The T cell differentiates directly into a memory cell

explanation.summary: Full activation of a naive T cell requires signal 1 (TCR recognition of peptide-MHC, shown with CD4/CD8 coreceptors) plus signal 2, costimulation via CD28 binding B7 (CD80/CD86) on the dendritic cell. If a T cell recognizes antigen without adequate costimulation, it is rendered anergic (or is deleted), a key mechanism of peripheral tolerance that prevents inappropriate activation against self-antigens presented in the absence of danger signals.
explanation.whyCorrect: Full activation of a naive T cell requires signal 1 (TCR recognition of peptide-MHC, shown with CD4/CD8 coreceptors) plus signal 2, costimulation via CD28 binding B7 (CD80/CD86) on the dendritic cell. If a T cell recognizes antigen without adequate costimulation, it is rendered anergic (or is deleted), a key mechanism of peripheral tolerance that prevents inappropriate activation against self-antigens presented in the absence of danger signals.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation
questions.stem: This figure shows a naive CD4+ T cell differentiating into distinct helper subsets depending on the cytokine environment, each producing characteristic effector cytokines and functions. Which subset, driven by IL-12 and secreting IFN-gamma, is most important for enhancing macrophage killing of intracellular bacteria?

explanation.summary: IL-12 (with IFN-gamma) drives Th1 differentiation; Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill ingested intracellular pathogens and promotes B-cell switching to opsonizing IgG. Th2 (IL-4) targets helminths and drives IgE; Th17 (IL-6, TGF-beta, IL-1) recruits neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi; Treg (TGF-beta, IL-2) suppresses responses and maintains tolerance.
explanation.whyCorrect: IL-12 (with IFN-gamma) drives Th1 differentiation; Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill ingested intracellular pathogens and promotes B-cell switching to opsonizing IgG. Th2 (IL-4) targets helminths and drives IgE; Th17 (IL-6, TGF-beta, IL-1) recruits neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi; Treg (TGF-beta, IL-2) suppresses responses and maintains tolerance.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation
questions.stem: This figure outlines the T-cell receptor signaling cascade: TCR/CD3 clustering, Lck-mediated phosphorylation and ZAP-70 recruitment, and downstream events that raise cytosolic calcium and activate transcription factors including NFAT, NF-kB, and AP-1. The rise in cytosolic calcium activates calcineurin, which in turn activates which transcription factor targeted by cyclosporine and tacrolimus?

explanation.summary: Increased cytosolic calcium activates the phosphatase calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT, allowing it to enter the nucleus and drive IL-2 transcription. The immunosuppressants cyclosporine and tacrolimus inhibit calcineurin, blocking NFAT activation and thereby suppressing T-cell activation, which is exploited to prevent transplant rejection. NF-kB and AP-1 are activated through the PKC and MAPK arms of the same cascade.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased cytosolic calcium activates the phosphatase calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT, allowing it to enter the nucleus and drive IL-2 transcription. The immunosuppressants cyclosporine and tacrolimus inhibit calcineurin, blocking NFAT activation and thereby suppressing T-cell activation, which is exploited to prevent transplant rejection. NF-kB and AP-1 are activated through the PKC and MAPK arms of the same cascade.

questions.stem: A naive CD4+ T cell differentiates into the subset shown, which secretes IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and drives IgE class switching, mast cell degranulation, eosinophil activation, and intestinal mucus/peristalsis. This response is MOST important for host defense against which of the following?

explanation.summary: The figure depicts Th2 differentiation and its effector arms (IL-4/5/13, IgE, eosinophils, mast cells, mucus and peristalsis). This program mediates immunity against helminths and, when dysregulated, causes allergic disease. Intracellular pathogens are handled by Th1/CD8 responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure depicts Th2 differentiation and its effector arms (IL-4/5/13, IgE, eosinophils, mast cells, mucus and peristalsis). This program mediates immunity against helminths and, when dysregulated, causes allergic disease. Intracellular pathogens are handled by Th1/CD8 responses.

questions.stem: The CD4+ Th1 cell activates the macrophage via CD40L-CD40 and IFN-gamma. What is the principal antimicrobial consequence of this activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgE class switching in B cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct antibody-mediated pore formation in bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enhanced killing of phagocytosed intracellular microbes

explanation.summary: Th1 cells license macrophages through CD40L-CD40 and IFN-gamma. The activated ('classically activated') macrophage generates ROS and NO to kill ingested microbes, secretes TNF/IL-1/IL-12, and upregulates MHC and B7.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th1 cells license macrophages through CD40L-CD40 and IFN-gamma. The activated ('classically activated') macrophage generates ROS and NO to kill ingested microbes, secretes TNF/IL-1/IL-12, and upregulates MHC and B7.

questions.stem: The CD8+ T cell kills the virus-infected cell using the receptor-ligand pair and downstream caspase shown, without releasing cytotoxic granules. This represents which of the following?

explanation.summary: FasL on the CTL engages Fas on the target, activating caspase-3 and apoptosis. This death-receptor pathway is an alternative to perforin/granzyme granule exocytosis and does not require granule contents.
explanation.whyCorrect: FasL on the CTL engages Fas on the target, activating caspase-3 and apoptosis. This death-receptor pathway is an alternative to perforin/granzyme granule exocytosis and does not require granule contents.

questions.stem: A CD8+ cytotoxic T cell recognizes a virus-infected cell via MHC I and releases the granule contents shown. What is the specific role of perforin in this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It forms pores in the target-cell membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cross-links Fas to trigger caspases

choices.label: E
choices.text: It fixes complement on the target membrane

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic granules contain perforin, granzymes, and serglycin. Perforin polymerizes to create pores that let granzymes enter the cytosol, where they activate caspases and induce apoptosis of the infected cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytotoxic granules contain perforin, granzymes, and serglycin. Perforin polymerizes to create pores that let granzymes enter the cytosol, where they activate caspases and induce apoptosis of the infected cell.

questions.stem: An antibody-coated tumor cell is recognized by the CD16 Fc receptor on the effector cell shown; Fc cross-linking triggers degranulation and the target dies by apoptosis. What is this killing mechanism called?

explanation.summary: NK cells express CD16 (FcγRIII), which binds the Fc region of IgG coating a target cell. Cross-linking triggers release of cytotoxic granules, killing the antibody-coated cell by ADCC. This differs from complement lysis and from phagocytosis.
